To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(1) the current state of practice of testing in open source software projects is poor and developers are not satisfied with the tools available to them; (2) developers have high expectations from bug localization techniques and they want to use a technique that is easy to use and gives accurate results; (3) developers want a tool that can help them find the elements they need to test; (4) practitioners suggest several characteristics for a good test case and we propose a technique to find good test cases.

(i) the current state of practice for testing in open source is far from perfect and practitioners face many challenges; (ii) there is a gap between practitioners' expectation from bug localization tools and what is currently available; (iii) there is a need to remove bias in data for bug localization techniques to give accurate and reliable results.

(1) Developers are not able to find bugs using current bug localization techniques, (2) Developers are not happy with the current state of practice and (3) Developers want a bug localization technique that can find bugs accurately, efficiently and can be used by non-expert developers.
